non_blocking: Cross-workspace compose project collision: `docker compose up -d`/`down` derive the project name from the basename of the project directory, and no `--project-name` is passed. Two workspaces whose project directory has the same basename (e.g. two repos both checked out under a dir named `app`) resolve to the same compose project; `down` in one workspace can tear down the other's containers. In a multi-tenant harness this is a real interference risk. Mitigation: derive a stable project name from the canonical workspace path or accept an optional `projectName` input.

Up/down project asymmetry: `path` given as a *file* (`-f <abs>`) and `path` given as a *directory* (`--project-directory <abs>`) can name different projects (and the directory form only works if the dir contains a default-named compose file). A caller that brings a project up with a file path and later tears it down with a directory path (or a differently-named compose file) silently targets a different or nonexistent project instead of failing loudly.

`docker_build` assumes any file path is a Dockerfile (`-f <file> <dirname>`). Passing a non-Dockerfile file (e.g. a compose file, README) yields a confusing docker parse error. Similarly, a non-existent build path is silently treated as a build-context directory, and a non-existent compose path is treated as a file (`-f <missing>`), producing generic docker errors rather than a precise ToolFailure.

Summary strings for `docker_compose_up`/`down` are hardcoded (`"compose project started"`) and ignore the actual number of services/containers reported in output; `up -d` returns before containers are healthy, so the success summary can claim started even if a container crashed immediately after.

Duplicate resolve logic: `docker_build` re-implements the `resolveInWorkspace` try/catch/statSync pattern instead of sharing a helper like `resolveComposeArgv`; the two copies can drift (they already differ slightly — one checks `isDirectory`, the other `isFile`).
security: Success-path output of the new network/state tools (`docker_build`, `docker_compose_up`, `docker_compose_down`) concatenates `stdout + stderr` into `raw` without passing it through `redactCredentials`; only the error paths (`firstErrorLine`/`toolFailure`) redact. If a build step or a registry pull/auth warning echoes a URL with embedded credentials (`https://token@host`, `user:pass@host`), the unredacted output reaches the model. This is consistent with the pre-existing read tools but is a higher-risk exposure for tools that pull/build over the network. `runDocker` also never passes the runner's `redact` option.

The entire security story of these tools rests on `ctx.permission.approved` being set by the DSH host only after genuine human approval. Per the DeepSeek Harness compatibility manifest, the permission hook API is explicitly `TBD — must be verified against the pinned commit`; the wiring is unverified. The plugin fails closed (safe), but the gate is either permanently non-functional (host never sets `ctx.permission`, so every state change is denied) or effectively a no-op (host sets `approved: true` for every tool call) depending on host behavior that is not exercised anywhere in this PR.

Workspace-controlled compose files / Dockerfiles are attacker-influenceable content that the harness reviews. `docker compose up` and `docker build` can bind-mount arbitrary host paths (e.g. `/:/mnt`), run privileged containers, add host networking, and mount the docker socket — full host compromise if the file is malicious. Acceptable only because of the approval gate; worth stating explicitly in tool descriptions and ensuring the approval UX shows the user the compose file before approval.

Compose project name can be influenced by a workspace `.env`/`name:` field in the compose file; combined with `docker compose down`, a malicious project can name itself to match and remove containers/networks of a different project. Again gated by approval, but the `down` tool is a broader hammer than `stop` and is classified as `system-change` even though removing containers is on the boundary of `destructive` (data in anonymous volumes is irreversibly lost).
test_gaps: No test asserts the exact argv constructed: `docker_build` file → `-f <abs> <dirname>`, directory → context, default → `workspaceRoot`; compose up/down → `-f <abs>` vs `--project-directory <abs>`. The mock runner returns the same output regardless of args, so a regression that, say, drops the `-f` flag or swaps the build context would pass silently.

No path-boundary / error-path tests for `docker_compose_up` and `docker_compose_down` (out-of-workspace path, leading-dash path, symlink loop, non-existent path) — only `docker_build` and `docker_compose_status` cover these.

Zero live (real docker) integration coverage for the three new state-changing tools. `docker_build`, `docker_compose_up`, and `docker_compose_down` are the most consequential tools in the plugin and their real-binary behavior is entirely untested.

The live `docker_compose_status` test was weakened in b8efc4e to `return` (silently pass) when `result.ok` is false, removing the `expect(result.ok).toBe(true)` assertion. On any environment where compose or `--format json` is broken, the test now passes trivially — it can no longer fail, so it provides no signal.

The permission-denied tests pass `approved=false`, which the `ctx()` helper maps to `permission: undefined` (relying on the plugin's `?? { approved: false }` default). There is no test with an explicit `{ approved: false }` context, and no test exercising the denial path for a path/tag that is also invalid (ordering of the PermissionDenied vs InvalidArguments branches).
No test asserts success-path output is credential-redacted (it currently is not, see security) — a redaction fix would have no regression coverage.
compatibility: Permission hook API unverified against the pinned DeepSeek Harness commit (manifest: `permission_hook_api: TBD`). These tools depend on `ctx.permission` being populated by the host, which is not confirmed; a contract-kit default of `{ approved: true }` masks this in tests.

Env allowlist (DEFAULT_ENV_ALLOWLIST) drops `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`, `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY`, `DOCKER_CERT_PATH`, and all `COMPOSE_*` variables. Docker still finds its default context via `HOME`/`USERPROFILE` config, so default-local-daemon setups work, but any environment relying on `DOCKER_HOST`/`DOCKER_CONTEXT` (remote/CI daemons, colima/podman over env) is silently ignored — the tool will act on the default context instead of the user's configured one. For state-changing tools this is a consequential silent misdirection.

`statSync`/`realpathSync`/`dirname` handling on Windows is correct (`resolveInWorkspace` normalizes backslashes), and the Windows-CI-specific compose quirks are the stated reason for the weakened live test; no new cross-platform defect found beyond the compose-availability variance the PR already tolerates.
architecture: Top-of-file module comment is now stale and factually wrong: it states "All tools are read-only" and "none of them modify state", and lists the tools without `docker_build`, `docker_compose_up`, `docker_compose_down`. This will mislead future maintainers about the plugin's trust boundary.

`capabilities` now lists both `read-only` and `system-change` together, which is semantically contradictory for a capability advertisement; consider a per-tool capability breakdown or a clearer taxonomy.

`docker_compose_down` sits on the destructive boundary (removes containers; anonymous-volume data irreversibly lost) but is classified `system-change`. Defensible, but only `down` (not the gentler `stop`) is exposed, so the least-reversible option is the only one available.

Ordering nit: permission is checked before tag/path validation in the new tools, so an invalid tag combined with no approval returns `PermissionDenied` rather than `InvalidArguments` — harmless but inconsistent with the validate-then-gate ordering used elsewhere.
